$doc: THE RAIL HANDOFF. Sixteen mutations against the four files that carry it. Loud ones prove a check exists; the boundary ones (R13, R14) prove it is CORRECT, and both were decided from the spec before the code was read back — the deadline extension may never shorten, and a reservation is valid AT its deadline (the house convention guardrails already uses for expires_at). R9 and R14 exist because writing this spec found two cases the suite could not see; the assertions that catch them (E11, C2a) were written for these mutations, not photographed from a passing run.

name: R1 the sweep ignores settlement (a settled spend is auto-reversed anyway)
R2 a submission does not extend the deadline (a slow success is still reversed under it)
from: else if (e.kind === 'submission') { const r = open.get(e.authId); if (r && e.expiresAt > r.deadline) r.deadline = e.expiresAt; }

name: R14 BOUNDARY: a reservation expires AT its deadline instead of after it
R5 the RAW settlement capability is written to the durable log (a leaked backup forges settlements)
R3 capabilityMatches accepts anything (any caller can cancel a reversal)
to:
if (presented) return true;
  const a = crypto.createHash('sha256').update(capabilityHash(authId, presented)).digest();

name: R4 the capability hash stops binding the authId (one token works on every authorization)
R13 BOUNDARY: a submission may SHORTEN a deadline (a rail can pull a reservation in early)
R8 a late settlement does not re-reserve (real money stays uncounted)
from: if (late) out.push(Object.assign({ kind: 'reservation' }, base, { amount: state.amount, reason: 'LATE_SETTLEMENT' }));
to: if (false) out.push(Object.assign({ kind: 'reservation' }, base, { amount: state.amount, reason: 'LATE_SETTLEMENT' }));

name: R9 a failed report reverses even when the TTL already did (budget credited TWICE for one payment)
from: if (state.reserved) out.push(Object.assign({ kind: 'reversal' }, base, { amount: state.amount, reason: 'RAIL_FAILED' }));
to: out.push(Object.assign({ kind: 'reversal' }, base, { amount: state.amount, reason: 'RAIL_FAILED' }));

name: R11 a settled report no longer needs a transaction id (a settlement naming nothing)
R6 every report is recorded as 'capability' (the operator claim is laundered into the stronger one)
R7 a contradicting second report is accepted (settled and failed both signed)
R10 the settlement reuses the authorization id (the report SHADOWS the ALLOW receipt it descends from)
R12 the receipt claims Cosmos observed the rail (the one thing it must never say)
from: { name: 'Rail outcome observed by Cosmos', pass: false }],
to: { name: 'Rail outcome observed by Cosmos', pass: true }],

name: R15 the schema is not bumped (an old verifier prints a tx id with no NOT-OBSERVED qualifier)
R16 rail_late is always false (the TTL's wrong guess is hidden from the auditor)

$doc: ROUND 2, after review (Ramu, 2026-09-08). R17-R22 cover the credential split, the schema-acceptance set and the overrun code. R19 is the most useful of them: it is the PARTIAL FIX a reader would write from the review message alone. The reviewer named `settled` as the danger; the severe direction is `failed`, because that one returns the budget and buys a double-spend. A fix that blocks only what the review named would pass every assertion written to that review's framing, so K1/K3 exist to catch it. R22 is the second boundary pair in this spec: spent EQUAL to budget is spent-out, not overrun, decided before the code was read back.

name: R17 THE DOUBLE-SPEND: the ALLOW holder may report `failed`, so it gets its own budget back and spends the same money twice
R18 the rail token alone settles, with no handoff check (a rail settles authorizations it was never given)
R19 THE PARTIAL FIX: `settled` is correctly restricted and `failed` is left open to everyone (the review named `settled`; `failed` is the severe direction)
R20 the verifier stops accepting older schemas (every receipt already in an audit file becomes unverifiable)
R21 an overrun grant reports INSUFFICIENT_BALANCE again (a reader is told to retry smaller, forever)
R22 BOUNDARY: spent EQUAL to budget is reported as overrun (a grant that did exactly what it was told reads as broken)
R23 the OPERATOR may report `failed` too (a credential with no route that credits a grant gains one)
R24 the ALLOW holder may report `settled` (it cannot take budget back, but it can certify its own payment)

$doc: ⚠ R17 and R19 SURVIVED a run of record on 2026-09-08 and the survival was MY doing, not a missing test: round 3 replaced the two `if` lines they were anchored to with the MAY_REPORT table, so `from` matched 0 times. mutate.js refused to apply them and counted them as survivors, which is the only reason it was noticed — had it skipped an unmatched mutation quietly, the run would have reported ALL CAUGHT while the two controls that prove the double-spend fix were dead. Re-anchored to the table. LESSON: a mutation spec is code that rots against the code it attacks, and 'the spec still parses' is not 'the spec still points at anything'.

name: R25 the rail's own state word is dropped (a Writ `reversed` becomes indistinguishable from a payment that never ran)
R26 rail_state is left out of the signed bytes (the fact survives only in the HTTP reply, which nobody archives)
R27 `reversed` is accepted as a Cosmos OUTCOME (the closed set stops being closed)

$doc: ⚠ SECOND TIME: R15 and R20 rotted again on 2026-09-09, against MY OWN schema 3->4 bump. This morning R17/R19 rotted the same way against my assertMayReport refactor. The lesson from that run said a mutation spec is code that rots against the code it attacks - and I still did not re-anchor these when I changed the exact lines they point at. mutate.js caught it BOTH times by refusing to apply an unmatched `from` and counting it SURVIVED, which is the only reason either was noticed. RULE: when you edit a line, grep this spec for it in the same commit.
